core: Working definition of an expense: the cost of resources used up to earn revenue
Expense recognition principle: recognized when incurred, not when paid
Expense versus asset: used up now versus a resource for later
Common types of expenses: rent, wages, materials, utilities, marketing
Expenses reduce owners' equity through the accounting equation
Expense versus liability: cost incurred versus amount owed
Controlling expenses: spending decisions, not just cuts
Honest framing: expenses are the price of earning
supporting: Budgeting as the planning and control tool for spending
Most, but not all, expenses are tax-deductible
outOfScope: Journal entries and posting mechanics (sibling topics)

claims.claim: Expenses are the cost of resources associated with earning revenues.
Under the expense recognition principle, expenses are recognized when they are incurred, not necessarily when they are paid.
An increase in expenses decreases retained earnings, which is part of owners' equity.
An expense flows to the income statement, whereas a capital expenditure is recorded on the balance sheet as an asset and expensed later (for example, through depreciation).
Common operating expenses include rent, wages and salaries, materials (cost of goods sold), utilities, and marketing.
On the income statement, expenses are deducted from revenue to arrive at net income; the balance sheet reports assets, liabilities, and equity at a point in time.
Budgeting is how a business plans and controls spending: a budget sets targets in advance, actual results are compared against them, and the business adjusts along the way.
Most, but not all, expenses are deductible in arriving at taxable income, and deductibility varies by jurisdiction.

conflictingEvidence.issue: When should an expense be recorded: when cash is paid or when the cost is incurred?
positions: Cash-basis accounting records expenses when cash is paid
Accrual accounting records expenses when they are incurred, matched to the revenue they help produce
conflictingEvidence.resolution: This lesson teaches the accrual treatment, which is the framework behind the income statement described by OpenStax and CFI. Cash accounting is a sibling topic and is referenced only.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is marketing an expense or an investment?
positions: Accounting records marketing costs as expenses in the period they are incurred
Some managers argue marketing builds future value, like an investment
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the accounting treatment as fact and frames the business judgment as a spending decision (a budget question), without claiming marketing is an asset.
